designCorrection.what: A mid-build correction, made before anything reached the factory side. The dispatch's literal one-line description of evaluateRailGate's fix ('a rail NOT in [the declared-ahead] set with zero earned cells in this county is a REFUSAL') would have refused every county OTHER than Travis for maxImperviousCoverPct -- a rail whose writer is deliberately hard-scoped to Travis only and never writes so much as a not-applicable cell anywhere else, a ratified design proven by hauska-factory test/gate-county-scoped-rail.test.mjs BEFORE this lane started. Caught by reading that test before implementing, not after.
designCorrection.fix: RAIL_NEVER_FILLED now fires ONLY when cells.length === 0 -- loadCountyRailCells guarantees this happens exclusively when the county itself has zero parcel_record rows (never instantiated), a genuine structural 'this county does not exist yet' signal. A populated county with zero earned cells for one rail is completely unchanged from pre-fix behavior (still excludedDeclaredAhead) -- this covers BOTH a genuinely never-built rail AND a rail deliberately scoped elsewhere, without needing to (and without being able to) distinguish them from cell data alone.

declaredAheadProgramWideLiveMeasurement.operationalNote: The full-table RAIL_LIVENESS_SQL scan takes ~52s against the live store on the read replica -- confirms the AGENT_CONTRACT section 4 heavy-scan concern was real, not theoretical, and validates computing it once per scheduler run (this measurement) rather than once per (county, rail) subprocess (would have been 52s x up to thousands of pairs). Also empirically demonstrated the risk directly: an early live run that omitted --declared-ahead (letting gate-rail-cli.mjs self-compute) hit the CLI's own 20s per-statement timeout and failed -- reproducing exactly the cost this design avoids.
